symptom: gitignore hid the deployed free catalogue
root_cause: The ignore patterns were written as "apps/" and "paid/" with no leading slash, and git matches an unanchored pattern at every depth. site/apps/ is the deployed free catalogue, so the Friday job's "git add -A" silently skipped the entire directory.
evidence: git check-ignore site/apps/probe/app/index.html returned 0 (ignored). Run 38311010124 committed data/candidate.json and no app.
repro: git check-ignore site/apps/probe/app/index.html
fix: Anchored both patterns as /apps/ and /paid/.
regression_test: selftest_audit.py
verification: selftest_audit passes; the guard was confirmed by reverting .gitignore and watching it report the problem.

symptom: committed state carried the build machine's absolute paths
root_cause: stage_app stored paid_dir and installer with str(path.resolve()), while the candidate field beside them was correctly relative. data/candidate.json is committed, so the Friday runner's own folder layout was published to every other machine, where it resolves to nothing.
evidence: data/candidate.json in 0274226 held "D:\a\Slingshot-Tools\Slingshot-Tools\paid\dev-converter".
repro: git show 0274226:data/candidate.json
fix: Both stored relative to the repo via _rel(), which reports a path outside the repo as empty rather than absolute.
regression_test: selftest_audit.py checks no tracked state file holds a Windows absolute path.
verification: selftest_audit reports 0 problems and the committed file now reads paid/dev-converter.

symptom: NSIS installed but makensis was not on PATH
root_cause: choco install nsis succeeds and writes the machine PATH, but a GitHub Actions step runs with the PATH it started with, so the install is invisible to the step that asked for it.
evidence: Run 38385940018: "The term 'makensis' is not recognized" on the line immediately after "The install of nsis was successful".
repro: gh run view 38385940018 --log-failed
fix: Both jobs resolve makensis.exe from its install location, print where it was found, fail with a real message if absent, and add the directory to GITHUB_PATH.
regression_test: verified by the next run reaching the installer step
verification: Run 38401429866 generated and committed; the generate job completed with makensis resolved.

symptom: rate limit backoff spent the whole retry budget inside one window
root_cause: A 429 slept 10s then 20s, but the allowance is per minute, so every attempt landed inside the same window and received the same refusal. The verifier then reported the app as unrepairable.
evidence: Run 38401720935: rounds 2 to 4 each failed with 429 on openai/gpt-oss-120b and ended "4 controls still dead".
repro: gh run view 38401720935 --log-failed
fix: _rate_limit_wait() waits out the meter's own window plus a margin, still growing so an exhausted key does not spin.
regression_test: stubbed sender: a 429 on the first two attempts returns the third successfully, after 65s then 90s
verification: verified locally with a stubbed provider

symptom: exposure gates refused the app the pipeline had just staged
root_cause: The generate job commits the free edition an hour before the verifier writes its catalog entry, so in between the app is in site/apps/ and in no catalog. Both gates read that as a leak and failed the run before the verifier could ever run.
evidence: Run 38400432942: "site/apps/dev-converter-basic is not a known free edition and must not be public".
repro: python check_repo_hygiene.py against the freshly generated app
fix: Both now read data/candidate.json and accept the app it names. Anything else, including a leftover from a retired product, is still reported.
regression_test: check_repo_hygiene.py and check_exposure.py both pass with the staged app present
verification: both scripts report ok

symptom: a generated app could not parse, so every control looked dead
root_cause: Three separate faults. make_app undid the model's JSON escaping one level at a time, so a doubly escaped reply kept its backslashes. Decoding only the quotes still left template literal markers escaped, which closes the template early. Independently, the model mistyped one closing delimiter. In each case the script block failed to parse, so no handler ran, so every control was reported dead, so the repair loop spent its budget patching controls that were never broken.
evidence: app_scanner on dev-converter: pageerror "Invalid or unexpected token", 6 of 6 controls dead.
repro: app_scanner.scan on the generated file
fix: _unescape() decodes the escapes a JSON string uses and repeats until stable; js_syntax_errors() checks every script block, using node when the runner has it and escaping plus delimiter checks when it does not; html_looks_fine() refuses to stage an app that cannot parse.
regression_test: jscheck_selftest.py proves the fallback does not cry wolf on ten valid snippets; audit_selftest.py checks the real generated app parses
verification: the next generate run reported "attempt 1 ok" and the app scans with 0 dead and 0 errors

symptom: the scanner refused working apps, so nothing could ever publish
root_cause: The probe demanded that clicking any control change the DOM, storage or an input value. Three classes of control cannot do that and are not broken: a select the app reads, a submit button in a form with required fields, and a button that opens a file picker.
evidence: dev-converter: dead=[4 controls] on an app that converts correctly.
repro: python app_scanner.py against the generated app
fix: An id the app's script reads is an input, not a button. Submit buttons get empty required fields filled first. The file inputs' click is intercepted, and a click that reached one is reported skipped.
regression_test: scanner_selftest.py builds a page with four genuinely broken controls, all of which must still be reported dead
verification: scanner_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. dev-converter: dead=[], skipped=['BUTTON:Import My Data']

symptom: the javascript check crashed on a Windows pipe
root_cause: The node branch passed the script as text, so the pipe encoded it with the runner's default codepage. An arrow character in the generated app raised UnicodeEncodeError in subprocess._stdin_write and the whole generate job died before the check could report anything.
evidence: Run 38400432942: UnicodeEncodeError, charmap codec cannot encode U+2192, in subprocess._stdin_write.
repro: the run log above
fix: The check encodes to UTF-8 itself and decodes the diagnostics the same way, so the codepage of whatever machine is running cannot change the verdict.
regression_test: nodecheck_selftest.py runs the node branch against a stub and fails if the arrow raises
verification: nodecheck_selftest.py: PASS

symptom: the paid publish outcome was recorded and then thrown away
root_cause: The step that records the itch.io outcome has no id, so the PUBLISHED value it writes to GITHUB_OUTPUT belongs to that step and is read by nothing. The job reports success whether or not the paid edition was actually published, which is the reporting defect the audit is required to eliminate.
evidence: Workflow inspection: the only step referencing steps.publish is the one that writes the unused output.
repro: python parse of friday-verify.yml
fix: The record step now has id: paid, writes the outcome to GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, and a final gate reads it. The gate runs after the free edition has been deployed, so one dead destination does not cost the customer the release that worked, but the job fails with a plain message. ALLOW_FREE_ONLY accepts the partial release deliberately.
regression_test: parsed friday-verify.yml; steps.paid exists and the gate is the final step
verification: Run 38416539839 executed the gate and reported the paid edition was not published, instead of reporting success. That is the first evidence the gate runs.

symptom: a debug backup file is committed to the published site
root_cause: qa_loop writes index.rN.bak beside the app it is repairing and nothing removes it. git add -A committed one into site/, which GitHub Pages serves. Development-only material shipped in a release.
evidence: git ls-files site/apps shows index.r3.bak
repro: git ls-files site/apps
fix: qa_loop writes per-round backups to data/qa_backups/ instead of beside the app, and check_exposure refuses to pass if any .bak, .trial.html, .py or .tmp reaches site/.
regression_test: planted index.r4.bak in the published tree; check_exposure reported it
verification: check_exposure ok after removal; index.r3.bak untracked and deleted

symptom: committed per-minute token counter was read as another runner's usage
root_cause: The Friday job's blanket git add committed data/token_usage.json. It is live rate-limit state for whichever machine is running, so each later run on another runner began its allowance from a total it did not earn.
evidence: Commit 0274226 contained data/token_usage.json with total 4370.
repro: git show --stat 0274226
fix: The file and its temporary siblings are ignored.
regression_test: cleanroom_selftest.py copies what git tracks and asserts it survives
verification: token_usage.json is ignored and untracked

symptom: an unreadable counter read as zero, so the pipeline kept spending
root_cause: _load() swallowed a parse error and returned {}, which spent() read as zero tokens used. affordable() then answered yes on every call. In a counter, zero is the answer that allows spending.
evidence: Executed the pre-fix module from 0274226 against a corrupt state file: spent=0, affordable(8000,100)=True.
repro: exec of git show 0274226:tokenmeter.py
fix: An unreadable or non-dict state is reported on stderr and read as unknown; spent() returns a figure above any limit. The write is atomic.
regression_test: audit_selftest.py writes truncated, list and numeric states and checks each is unknown, not zero, and leaves nothing affordable
verification: audit_selftest.py: FAILURES: none

symptom: an unreadable budget read as zero hours, so jobs were approved
root_cause: The same fail-open shape. A corrupt budget.json returned an empty budget, which read as a month with nothing spent, so check() approved work on a month that may already have spent all thirty hours. The module docstring claimed the hours were committed and could not quietly reset, which was false: 380e29e had deliberately untracked the file.
evidence: Executed the pre-fix module from 0274226: check() returned 0 (approved) with a corrupt state.
repro: exec of git show 0274226:budget.py
fix: check() refuses outright when the hours cannot be read; the write is atomic; the docstring describes what is actually true.
regression_test: audit_selftest.py checks a readable budget approves and corrupt ones refuse
verification: audit_selftest.py: FAILURES: none

symptom: a release could die on a traceback and still have claimed to save
root_cause: save() logged its success line before writing, and neither it nor publish_public() caught the write error, so an unattended job exited on a traceback and main() returned 0 either way.
evidence: Executed the pre-fix module against a read-only state file and against a read-only public file: PermissionError traceback, exit 1.
repro: exec of git show 0274226:update_state.py in a copied tree
fix: Both report whether they wrote, neither claims a save it cannot prove, and main() exits non-zero when either failed.
regression_test: audit_selftest.py makes the state file read-only and checks no traceback, a non-zero exit and no claimed save
verification: audit_selftest.py: FAILURES: none

symptom: the site advertised a paid product that was not for sale
root_cause: set_itch_url.valid() required at least one path segment, computed as len(path.strip('/').split('/')) >= 1. An account front page has the path '/', so strip gives the empty string, and ''.split('/') is [''], which has length one and passed. The catalog therefore held the account page as the product URL, publish_paid.py saw a URL present and a price in range, and set published=True.
evidence: The live store was fetched during the audit and lists zero products. site/apps.json carried published=true with itch_url pointing at the account page, and e2e_product.py reported the catalog as published while the itch.io check failed.
repro: python publish_paid.py password-manager, which exited 0 and left the tier marked published
fix: valid() now requires a non-empty first path segment and an account subdomain. publish_paid.py refuses on the same ground and then fetches the page, refusing to mark anything on sale unless the response contains a purchase or download section. The catalog was corrected: the paid tier is published=false with an empty itch_url until a real product page exists.
regression_test: itchurl_selftest.py
verification: itchurl_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. publish_paid.py password-manager now exits 1 with a plain message. check_exposure ok.
uncertainty: The upload to itch.io has still never been executed, because the credentials exist only as repository secrets. That the store is empty is confirmed by fetching the live page.

symptom: the installer job built the wrong product because a slug went stale
root_cause: build_paid_only took the slug from data/published.json, which the verify job writes and which was committed. Two dispatches in quick succession left published.json naming dev-converter while the artifact uploaded in that run held unit-converter, so the installer job looked for a directory that had never been uploaded.
evidence: Run 38416539839 failed with "no paid build at paid/dev-converter". Downloading the paid-build artifact from that same run shows unit-converter/app/index.html and nothing named dev-converter, so the correct build was present and was simply not the one it looked for.
repro: gh run download 38416539839 -n paid-build, then compare what arrived with what data/published.json named
fix: When the recorded slug has no build, exactly one uploaded build is used and the mismatch is logged and recorded as RETRIED. Two or more is ambiguous and is refused rather than guessed. data/published.json is untracked, because the artifact is the authority on what was actually built and carrying the slug through git only risks it being one release stale.
regression_test: paidbuild_selftest.py
verification: paidbuild_selftest.py: FAILURES: none, covering the named build, the stale-slug fallback, the ambiguous refusal, and no builds at all.
uncertainty: The itch.io upload is still unexecuted; the credentials exist only as repository secrets.

symptom: itch.io publishing reported success for having done nothing
root_cause: itch_publish.main() returned 0 when there was no data/published.json, printing 'nothing was built this week'. The release gate reads the step outcome, so 0 became PUBLISHED=yes, and the run summary printed 'the paid edition is on itch.io and advertised'. No request was ever made to itch.io.
evidence: Run 38424937223 is the proof. Its log contains '[itch] nothing was built this week', then 'PUBLISHED: yes', then 'paid edition is on itch.io and advertised'. Fetching https://slingshot-tools.itch.io/ after that run showed the store still listing no products at all. The gate was working correctly and was fed a lie.
repro: python itch_publish.py with no paid build and no stage file, which exited 0
fix: Doing nothing now exits 1 and says so. When the stage file is absent but exactly one paid build exists, that build is published using the title from its own concept.json, so an untracked stage file no longer stops the release. More than one build is ambiguous and is refused.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none, covering no build at all, more than one build, the real module's own output, and that the gate still keys off the real exit code.
uncertainty: The upload itself still needs the repository secrets; what is fixed is that the system can no longer claim it happened when it did not.

symptom: a quiet week stopped the website being deployed
root_cause: sync_links calls shorts_script.product() to build a sample YouTube description for a person to read. That helper raises SystemExit when there is no product to advertise, and the SystemExit propagated out of sync_links and failed the Pages job. Between releases there is always no product to advertise, so the site was only deployable in the window right after a release.
evidence: Run 38428458061 failed at 'Refresh the platform links' with '[shorts] no product record; nothing to advertise' and exit code 1, and no deploy step ran.
repro: gh workflow run pages.yml, which failed at the same step
fix: The sample is skipped when there is nothing to say and sync_links exits zero. A missing product is the normal case between releases.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py runs sync_links.py and checks the exit code
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. Run 38429073380 deployed the site successfully.

symptom: the itch.io session cookie is expired, so nothing can be uploaded
root_cause: itch.io sits behind a Cloudflare Turnstile bot challenge. A headless browser is served a 'Just a moment...' interstitial with a single hidden cf-turnstile-response input instead of the login form, so the permanent-credentials login cannot run at all. Getting past a bot check is evading an anti-abuse control, which this will not do, so the expiring session cookie remains the only way in and a person must supply it.
evidence: Run 38592104107: 'the login form was not what was expected' followed by 'the page is titled 'Just a moment...' and has 1 input(s): cf-turnstile-response'. The page it wanted to fill was never a form.
repro: gh run view 38592104107 --log
fix: The premise was wrong, and that is what was fixed. Uploading does not depend on the session cookie: butler authenticates with the API key, and the key is confirmed working. The expired cookie never blocked a scheduled release and was only ever a fallback for creating the first project.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py
verification: Run 38630319521: butler reached the itch.io builds endpoint with the key and was refused only because the project does not exist (400 invalid game), while the cookie check reported REFUSED in the same run. The upload path does not use the cookie.
uncertainty: Retired as disproven rather than fixed. The cookie is still expired and still unusable, and is retained only for the one-time project creation.

symptom: no product has ever been uploaded to itch.io
root_cause: Every path to a first upload requires a valid session cookie, which is blocked above. Until one product is uploaded there is nothing to sell, and the customer purchase journey cannot complete.
evidence: https://slingshot-tools.itch.io/ was fetched during this audit and lists no products. site/apps.json marks every paid tier published=false with an empty itch_url, which is the truth and is what the fixes made it say.
repro: webfetch https://slingshot-tools.itch.io/
fix: The store holds a product. set_itch_url.py --all points the paid editions at the one project and deliberately leaves the free editions without a store URL, because they are served from this site and were never uploaded to itch.io.
regression_test: itchurl_selftest.py asserts the catalog never claims to be on sale
verification: https://slingshot-tools.itch.io/slingshot-tools answers HTTP 200 and lists Chess clock-Setup.exe, which the pipeline uploaded unaided. The catalogue records the paid edition of chess-clock as published with its itch.io URL.
uncertainty: The purchase itself has not been completed, because that would mean paying for it. The link, the price and the build behind it are verified.

symptom: a price could be set below the hard floor and could never be sold
root_cause: charm() subtracts a cent unconditionally and was applied after clamp(), so charm(clamp(1.00)) is 0.99. publish_paid.py and itch_publish.record() both refuse any price outside $1-$10, so a product nudged to $0.99 could never be listed. Worse, decide() signals a hold by returning the current price, so every run also applied charm to a price that had been decided not to move, sliding it down a cent per run for ever, and writing audit-log entries that read 'held' beside a price that had moved.
evidence: Executed over the full legal range: charm(clamp(1.00)) == 0.99, below FLOOR, and 323 of 901 legal price points had a float delta of at least 0.01 against the held price.
repro: python -c 'import pricing; pricing.charm(pricing.clamp(1.00))'
fix: A hold now returns before charm is applied, so the price stays exactly where it was. Clamp happens after charm, never before, and the comparison is rounded to cents so a float artefact cannot rewrite a price.
regression_test: property_selftest.py
verification: property_selftest.py: no failure across 4505 decide/clamp/charm cases; ten idle runs leave the price at $3.00 and a real cut and raise still move it.

symptom: loading the release state destroyed the per-app version map
root_cause: load() coerced both 'apps' and 'next_major_notes' to lists. 'apps' is a dict of slug to version, so every load replaced it with an empty list.
evidence: Reproduced: a state file with apps={'password-manager': '1.4.0'} loaded to apps=[], app_version() then answered 2.0.0, the company-wide version, and set_app_version() raised TypeError: list indices must be integers.
repro: python -c 'import update_state; s=update_state.load()' against a state file with a populated apps map
fix: Each key is coerced to its own type, dict for apps and list for notes.
regression_test: audit_selftest.py
verification: apps survives load(), app_version() returns the recorded version and set_app_version() adds without raising.

symptom: a failed installer build returned the previous release's binary
root_cause: The NSIS return code was never checked. Only the existence of the output file was, and dist/ kept the previous release's installer, so a compile error, a timeout or a full disk still found last week's file and returned it while printing 'installer built'. build_paid_only.plausible() only checks size and the MZ header, which a genuine but outdated binary passes.
evidence: The code read 'if not out_exe.exists()' with no test of r.returncode anywhere before it.
repro: the branch as written
fix: The previous installer is removed before the build, the exit status is checked, and a failed build also unlinks any partial output. The file's existence now means this build produced it.
regression_test: audit_selftest.py checks the return code is examined and the unlink happens before the build
verification: Both confirmed by reading the compiled source.

symptom: shorts captions were placed outside the clip they belong to
root_cause: _words_from_text already returns offsets in seconds, matching the ElevenLabs alignment path. The estimate path then multiplied them by the clip duration a second time.
evidence: Executed: a 3.0 second line of six words produced offsets [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5] and then [0.0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6.0, 7.5], so the last caption fired 4.5 seconds after the clip ended. Nothing logged it.
repro: python -c 'import shorts_voice as s; print(s._words_from_text("a b c", 3.0))'
fix: The offsets are rounded and used as they come.
regression_test: audit_selftest.py
verification: Offsets for 1, 3 and 10 second lines all fall inside their clip.

symptom: a video shorter than its narration lost the call to action
root_cause: The frame list was trimmed or padded in memory and then discarded. ffmpeg is given the '%05d.jpg' pattern and reads however many files are on disk, so the adjustment changed nothing and -shortest then cut the audio to the shorter video.
evidence: The log line 'trim or extend frames: have 880, need 918' was printed while the directory still held 880 files. The only trace of the problem was a reassuring message.
repro: read the source: the adjusted list had no reader after the assignment
fix: The trim and the pad happen on disk, the resulting count is verified and reported, and padding continues the ffmpeg numbering from have + 1 because starting at have overwrote the last real frame.
regression_test: checked directly over five trim and pad cases
verification: 5->8, 8->3, 880->918, 918->880 and 10->10 all reach the exact count, and the padded tail is the real final frame.

symptom: no itch.io project exists to upload to
root_cause: Uploading needs a project, and itch.io has no endpoint for creating one: every listing path answers 'invalid api endpoint', and the web login that would create it is behind a Cloudflare Turnstile bot challenge. Getting past a bot check is evading an anti-abuse control, which this will not do. The API key is confirmed working, so this is the last thing standing between the pipeline and a live store.
evidence: Run 38630319521: 'The API key works', and butler reached '/wharf/builds: invalid game' for a project name that does not exist. Runs 38592104107 and later: the login page is a 'Just a moment...' interstitial with one cf-turnstile-response input, not a form.
repro: gh run view 38630319521 --log
fix: The project was created once by the account holder, as the only manual step the store requires. Everything after that is automated: the store project is configuration rather than catalogue content, so a product the catalogue has never seen resolves to it, and the upload target is taken from the page rather than the product's name.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py
verification: Run 38806231965 succeeded end to end. publish() resolved the store project, confirmed the page answered, butler pushed to slingshot-tools/slingshot-tools:windows-64 with the API key, the page still answered, and the product was marked published on the site at $3.00. The paid release gate passed.
uncertainty: itch.io still exposes no endpoint for creating a project, so this will need repeating only if the store is ever recreated.

symptom: the itch.io session cookie is expired
root_cause: This was believed to block all uploading. It does not. butler authenticates with the API key, which is confirmed working, so no session is needed for a release at all and the expired cookie is irrelevant to the paid path. It is kept only as the fallback for the one-time project creation that the key cannot do.
evidence: Run 38630319521: butler reached the itch.io builds endpoint with the key and was refused only because the project does not exist, while the cookie check still reported REFUSED.
repro: gh run view 38630319521 --log
fix: The upload path no longer depends on the cookie, so its expiry blocks nothing that runs on a schedule.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py
verification: The doctor distinguishes the two: the key is accepted, the session is not needed.
uncertainty: The cookie's expiry is expected and is no longer treated as a defect in the release path.

symptom: butler was reported missing while sitting in the repository
root_cause: butler() looked in ~/.butler and on PATH only. butler.exe is committed in ./butler, and the workflow extracts the downloaded copy over that same folder, so the one tool the store depends on was being reported absent while present in the working directory. upload() logs 'butler is not installed' and returns False, which reads like a missing dependency rather than a wrong search path.
evidence: Run 38624142147 logged 'butler is not on this machine, so the key cannot be tested' while actions/checkout had just restored butler/butler.exe.
repro: place a file at butler/butler.exe and call itch_publish.butler()
fix: butler() now checks ~/.butler, ./butler, the repository root and ./bin, each with the platform's executable name, before falling back to PATH.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py, plus a direct check that a file at butler/butler.exe is found
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. The direct check returned <repo>\butler\butler.exe.

symptom: the API key was passed to butler as a flag that does not exist
root_cause: upload() passed --api_key. butler v15 has no such flag under that spelling or the hyphenated one, and prints 'unknown long flag' then exits 1 before making any network request. The key was therefore never presented to itch.io and no upload could ever have authenticated, whatever the key's real value was.
evidence: 'butler.exe : butler: error: unknown long flag' reproduced locally against the committed butler v15.32.0 for both --api_key and --api-key.
repro: & butler\butler.exe push src tgt --api_key dummy
fix: The key is handed over in BUTLER_API_KEY, which is what butler's own CI notice recommends, so it also stays out of the process list that every other process on the runner can read.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. The flag was confirmed absent and the environment route confirmed accepted by butler.

symptom: the upload target named a channel itch.io does not have
root_cause: ITCH_CHANNEL defaulted to the bare word 'windows'. butler requires the target as user/slug:channel and rejects the name outright with 'invalid spec ... missing channel', before any request, so every push died on the local validation of its own arguments.
evidence: Locally, butler answered 'invalid spec: slingshot-tools/probe, missing channel (examples: ...:windows-32-beta, ...:linux-64)'.
repro: & butler\butler.exe push stub.zip user/project
fix: The default is windows-64, itch.io's own Windows channel, and it stays overridable through ITCH_CHANNEL.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none.

symptom: the doctor's reading of butler inverted the answer it was measuring
root_cause: The classifier called the result REFUSED whenever the text contained 'invalid'. butler's answer for a perfectly good key and an unknown project is 'itch.io API error (400): /wharf/builds: invalid game'. That is the key working: the request reached the builds endpoint and only the project name was wrong. The rule reported a valid key as refused, which would have sent this looking for a bad secret that was not bad.
evidence: Run 38628290009 logged 'itch.io API error (400): /wharf/builds: invalid game' followed by '-> the key is REFUSED by itch.io'.
repro: read the classifier's condition and compare it with that error string
fix: Refusal is now 401, 403 or an explicit auth complaint. A 400 'invalid game', a 404 or 'not found' is read as the key being accepted and the project being absent, which is the distinction being measured.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py
verification: Run 38630319521 reported 'The API key works. Upload is therefore fully automated and needs no session at all.'

symptom: the doctor pushed its probe with the arguments the wrong way round
root_cause: butler reads 'push <src> <target>'. The probe passed the project name as the source and the stub file as the target, so butler tried to walk a project name as a directory and failed with 'open slingshot-tools/...: The system cannot find the path specified' before contacting itch.io. The probe could not have answered the question it exists to answer.
evidence: The identical failure reproduced locally against the committed butler before the order was corrected.
repro: & butler\butler.exe push user/project stub.zip
fix: The stub is the source and user/project:windows-64 is the target.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py
verification: Run 38630319521 reached the builds endpoint and returned the 400, which is only possible once the argument order is right.

symptom: publish asked the browser for a session that the API key does not need
root_cause: Step 1 of publish() asked find_game() whether the project already existed. find_game() reads the itch.io listing API, and every path on that API answers 'invalid api endpoint', so it always returned nothing. That sent every release down the browser-creation path, which needs a session, which the bot challenge refuses. The run therefore died asking for a cookie while holding a working API key, and never once attempted the upload the key was obtained for.
evidence: Run 38636758615: '[itch] no usable itch.io session could be established' and 'set ITCH_LOGIN and ITCH_PASSWORD once', while the doctor in the same run reported 'The API key works'.
repro: call publish() for a slug whose project exists, with no KEY and no session available
fix: Existence is decided from what can be trusted: the catalogue entry's itch_url when its public page answers, and only then the API. A live catalogue entry goes straight to the upload, so no session is looked for. Only a genuinely absent project now needs the browser, and that message names the one-time manual step instead of asking for a credential that would not have helped.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py asserts working_session() is never called when the catalogue points at a live page
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. The test fails if the catalogue lookup is removed.
uncertainty: The API listing endpoint remains unreadable, so find_game() is kept as a fallback but is no longer the only way existence is decided.

symptom: each release deleted the previous product's build from the store
root_cause: Every product was pushed to the same channel, windows-64, inside the one shared project. An itch.io channel holds a single build, so each weekly release replaced the one before it. After three successful runs the store listed only the newest build while the catalogue still advertised all three as purchasable, so a customer could pay for a download that was no longer there. That is worse than the empty store this audit spent its effort on: an empty shop is honest, a shop selling what it no longer has is not.
evidence: After run 38900671183 the project page listed only 'Base64 and URL encoding tool-Setup.exe', while the catalogue marked chess-clock, markdown-preview and base64-tool as published, so two of the three had nothing to download.
repro: publish two different products into the shared project and fetch the page afterwards
fix: Each product gets its own channel, derived from its slug, so the builds accumulate instead of overwriting. ITCH_CHANNEL still overrides it for anyone who wants a single channel, and the workflow no longer pins a channel that would defeat the per-product default.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py asserts two products resolve to two different channels, and that no workflow pins one
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. butler accepted a per-product channel name and refused only on the deliberately dummy key with 403, which is the refused-key shape rather than a bad-channel one.
uncertainty: The builds already overwritten are gone from the store and have to be put back by publishing those products again.

symptom: record() put a store URL on the free edition of a published product
root_cause: record() wrote itch_url onto every entry of the family, the free basic edition included, each time a product was published. The free edition is served from this site and is never uploaded to itch.io, so the catalogue claimed it was on a store it had never reached. set_itch_url.py --all had already been corrected for this, but record() is the path that runs on every release, so the correction never held.
evidence: site/apps.json carried itch_url on base64-tool-basic and markdown-preview-basic, both free editions whose paid siblings were published.
repro: publish a product and read the free edition's itch_url
fix: record() writes the URL to the paid edition only and clears any stale one from the free edition, so the catalogue cannot claim a free app is on itch.io.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py asserts no free edition of a published product carries a store URL
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none, and the catalogue was cleaned and re-checked.

symptom: one unlucky request deleted a project that existed
root_cause: page_is_live made a single request and treated anything other than 200 as proof the project did not exist, including a 429 and a timeout. itch.io rate-limits, and four consecutive probes of the same live page returned True, False, True, False. The publish path turned one of those into 'the store project did not answer', fell through to browser project creation, and told the account holder to go and create a project they had already created and that had been uploaded to twice.
evidence: Run 38912830336: '1. the store project did not answer' followed by 'no project exists and one cannot be created from here'. Concurrently on the same URL, page_probe returned True, False, True, False.
repro: call page_is_live on the live store project several times in a row
fix: The probe now distinguishes a verdict from a refusal. 403 and 404 are verdicts, so the page genuinely is not there; 429, 5xx and transport errors are refusals and are retried with backoff. If the store never answers, the run stops and says the store declined to answer, which is not the same as saying it does not exist.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py drives a probe that declines twice then answers, and one that never answers
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. It is probed three times and concluded live, and four times before giving up when it never answers.

symptom: two products were on sale with no download behind them
root_cause: Step 4 asked only whether the project page answered. The store is one project holding every product, so it answers perfectly well while missing the particular build being sold. chess-clock and markdown-preview had been published before builds got their own channel; their builds were replaced by later releases and the catalogue kept offering them, which is taking money for a download that cannot be delivered.
evidence: The store listed 'Base64 and URL encoding tool-Setup.exe' and 'Offline password manager-Setup.exe' while the catalogue marked chess-clock and markdown-preview as published. build_is_listed confirmed chess-clock's file is absent.
repro: publish a product, then replace its build, and check whether the site still offers it
fix: Publishing now verifies that this product's own installer file is listed on the page before it is advertised, retried because itch.io publishes builds asynchronously after the upload returns. The two orphans were taken off sale, since nothing can restore them without rebuilding those products and advertising them is worse than not offering them.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py asserts the step-4 check exists and that no advertised paid product lacks a build
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. The store now lists a build for every product on sale.
uncertainty: chess-clock and markdown-preview will return to the shop if and when the pipeline builds them again.

symptom: the builder could upload one product's installer as another's
root_cause: find_existing returned the first plausible *-Setup.exe anywhere in dist/, which is a folder shared by every build, with no regard for which product the file belonged to. Building chess-clock reused invoice-maker-Setup.exe. The publisher's find_installer had the same shape, falling back to `needle in stem or stem in needle`, a substring test in both directions. Either one sells a customer the wrong tool under the name they paid for.
evidence: python rebuild_paid.py chess-clock reported 'ready for itch.io: dist\invoice-maker-Setup.exe' for a product it had just reconstructed as chess-clock. dist/ held eleven installers, none of them chess-clock's.
repro: put another product's installer in dist/ and build this product
fix: find_existing only accepts a dist installer whose normalised name is this product's, and find_installer no longer falls back to a substring match at all. A missing installer stops the release, which is recoverable; shipping the wrong tool is not.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py puts a foreign installer in dist/ and checks neither the builder nor the publisher will take it
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none.

symptom: importing a module created directories in the repository
root_cause: itch_login.py called mkdir on .sessions and .cookies at module level, so merely importing it, including from a check that never runs the login, put two folders in the working tree. This is the general shape of the defect that started this audit's catalogue incident: a file nobody intended to write appearing in the tree.
evidence: prove_everything.py reported 'itch_login.py (mkdir)' as the one module that wrote to disk on import, twice, once for each directory.
repro: import itch_login with .sessions and .cookies absent and check whether they appear
fix: Both directories are created where they are written, inside the function that needs them, not on import.
regression_test: prove_everything.py, which checks every module for writes at import
verification: prove_everything.py: 0 BROKEN. Importing itch_login now creates neither directory.

symptom: generating the audit report took twenty-three minutes
root_cause: The report runs the whole suite, including cleanroom, and then write_report() called main() a second time to capture its output. Every check therefore ran twice, so a document that reads as a summary cost more than twenty minutes and would time out in CI.
evidence: Timed at 1410s before and 654s after, with run_selftests.py at 330s and cleanroom_selftest.py at 284s being paid for twice.
repro: time python audit_report.py
fix: The output of the single run is captured once and written from that, so the checks run one time. --quick leaves out the live customer journeys as well, for anyone who wants the document without the network.
regression_test: prove_everything.py runs it as an entry point and reports how long it took
verification: prove_everything.py: EXECUTED, rc=0 in 554.6s.
uncertainty: The report is still a heavy thing to generate because it genuinely runs the suite; --quick is the fast path.

symptom: a product's own installer could not be found under the name it shipped as
root_cause: Two builders name their output differently: make_app.py writes '<slug>-Setup.exe' and build_installer_app.py writes '<title>-Setup.exe'. find_installer matched only the slug and find_existing matched only paid.name, so neither recognised a title-named installer - which is the form actually on the store. find_installer('base64-tool') and find_installer('password-manager') both returned None while the store was selling 'Base64 and URL encoding tool-Setup.exe' and 'Offline password manager-Setup.exe'. The knock-on effect is worse than a failed lookup: rebuild_paid.py asks find_installer for the file it just built, so it would have reported that a live product 'cannot be reconstructed' and left it off the shelf indefinitely.
evidence: find_installer('password-manager') returned None next to a dist/ folder holding 'Offline password manager-Setup.exe', its live build.
repro: ask find_installer and find_existing for a product whose installer is named after its title
fix: Both now match the slug and the title, derived from paid/<slug>/concept.json and the catalogue, each still as an exact match so a foreign installer cannot be substituted. find_existing also had to normalise the whole file name rather than Path.stem, because _norm strips 'setup.exe' and the stem had already removed the '.exe', leaving a trailing 'setup' that matched nothing.
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py checks a title-named installer is found for its own product and that a foreign one beside it is not
verification: itchpublish_selftest.py: FAILURES: none.

symptom: the paid edition could be unlocked by adding ?paid to the free app's URL
root_cause: Twenty-five free editions were generated with `const PAID = new URLSearchParams(location.search).has('paid')` feeding the limit table, so the paid edition was the same file with nothing else standing between a visitor and the full product except a query string. Adding ?paid to the free app's own URL unlocked it. Every one of those twenty-five apps is a paid product and two of them, password-manager and base64-tool, are on the store for $3, so the bypass was live and free to anyone who guessed the parameter. The current generator bakes the edition in as TIER at build time instead, and rebuild_paid.py produces the full edition by flipping that one constant, so there is no runtime switch to reach.
evidence: the live free app at .../apps/password-manager-basic/ contained `const PAID=new URLSearchParams(location.search).has('paid');const LIM=PAID?{max:Infinity,export:true}:...`, so ?paid was the whole lock.
repro: append ?paid to a free edition's URL and read its limit table
fix: All twenty-five were rewritten to decide from TIER, not from the URL: `const LIM=TIER==='full'?{unlimited}:{basic}`. Flipping TIER to full still yields the paid edition, so rebuild_paid.py is unaffected, and the free edition is now genuinely limited with no way to reach the full one from the address bar.
regression_test: tier_gate_selftest.py reads every free edition and fails if any gates on the query string, or is labelled basic without a real limit table, or does not flip to a different full edition
verification: tier_gate_selftest.py: 34 free editions, FAILURES: none. Injecting the exploit back into one app makes it fail, so the test bites.

symptom: a successful paid build reported a failure after the installer was made
root_cause: build() logged where it had kept the installer with kept.relative_to(Path.cwd()). When the job runs from a different working directory than the repository, which is how CI invokes it, the installer is not under the cwd and relative_to raises ValueError. The exception came after the installer had been built and copied, so a finished build was reported as a crash and the release was abandoned with a valid installer sitting on disk.
evidence: python build_paid_only build() from a different cwd raised ValueError: 'paid\password-manager\Offline password manager-Setup.exe' is not in the subpath of the current directory, after printing 'installer built (19.6 MB)'.
repro: run the paid build with a working directory outside the repository
fix: The path is shown relative to the repository when it is inside it, and as an absolute path when it is not, with no exception either way.
regression_test: paidbuild_selftest.py builds a paid edition and checks it is kept
verification: paidbuild_selftest.py: FAILURES: none.

symptom: the release countdown was a day out for part of every day
root_cause: days_until, which phase() and therefore the banner, the Discord event and the trailer all read, computed its answer with now().date(). now() is UTC, while _empty() stamps date.today() and every other function in update_state reads the local calendar day. In any positive-offset timezone there is an hour each night where the two dates differ, and in that hour the countdown was one day long and the phase was wrong: on the release day itself phase returned 'announced' instead of 'live', so the countdown would not read zero on the day and the Discord event and the trailer would disagree about whether it had shipped. The suite could not pass on a clean checkout during that hour, which is how it was found.
evidence: property_selftest.py failed five date checks on a clean checkout at 2026-10-21 00:19 local, when UTC was still 2026-10-20: 'a date 100 days out is idle and 100 days away' reported 'idle / 101' and 'the day itself is live' reported 'announced'.
repro: run the date checks at a moment when the local date and the UTC date differ
fix: days_until uses date.today(), the same calendar day the rest of the module uses, so the countdown, the phase, the banner and the state's own timestamp agree at every hour.
regression_test: property_selftest.py now pins the two clocks together: a release 30 days out must report 30, whatever the hour
verification: property_selftest.py: FAILURES: none. Restoring now().date() makes the new check fail along with the five originals, so it bites.

symptom: the scheduled lanes died on a missing dependency before doing any work
root_cause: selftest.py imports every project module to prove they load, and one of them, update_trailer_render, imports pillow at module level; the same selftest parses every workflow with yaml. Five scheduled lanes installed requests alone, so they crashed on 'No module named PIL' and then 'No module named yaml' before running a single real check. The daily self-improvement lane, the weekly patch lane, the Wednesday review and the connections check had all been failing that way in every retained run, so the production pipeline was dead while the suite it could not reach stayed green on a developer machine that happened to have the libraries installed.
evidence: gh run list showed daily-improve failing every retained run back to 2026-10-13, each in about 13 seconds; gh run view --log-failed showed 'FAIL modules import ModuleNotFoundError: No module named PIL' and 'FAIL workflows parse ModuleNotFoundError: No module named yaml'.
repro: install requests alone in a fresh venv and run selftest.py, which is what the lanes did: 11/13 pass, both failures are the missing modules
fix: the five lanes install pillow and pyyaml alongside requests, the set the tests actually import.
regression_test: tracked_selftest.py now reads each workflow's install step and fails if a workflow that runs selftest.py does not install pillow and pyyaml
verification: a fresh venv with requests alone reproduces 11/13; adding pillow and pyyaml makes selftest.py and every other script the lanes run exit 0. Removing a dependency from a workflow makes the new check fail, so it bites.

symptom: the test suite posted a real announcement to the real Discord server
root_cause: update_selftest.py called update_discord.upsert() and expected it to return False because there are no credentials. The credentials are read from the environment when discord_post is imported, and a scheduled runner has DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN and DISCORD_GUILD_ID set, so on the runner the check created a real scheduled guild event and then failed, because the call returned True. The test was testing the ambient environment rather than the guard, and it was the only thing standing between the suite and the live server. Run 39640947607 is the evidence: the log reads 'created event 1562512689769484331' and then 'FAIL upsert without credentials is safe'.
evidence: gh run view 39640947607 --log showed '[event] created event 1562512689769484331 for 2026-10-26T18:00:00+00:00: Major update' immediately before the failing check, so the test really did create the event rather than merely report that it might.
repro: run update_selftest.py with DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN and DISCORD_GUILD_ID set
fix: the test forces dp.TOKEN and dp.GUILD_ID to empty for the duration of the check and restores them afterwards, so it tests the guard and cannot reach Discord whatever the machine has.
regression_test: update_selftest.py now clears both credentials around the check and restores them in a finally block, and the check still fails if the guard is removed
verification: with dummy credentials set the test passes and prints no 'created event' line, so the server is not touched; without the credentials cleared it creates a real event, which is what the old code did.

symptom: the test suite could have pushed a real build to the real store
root_cause: itchpublish_selftest.py starts itch_publish.py as a subprocess with the inherited environment and the real repository as its working directory. itch_publish reads ITCH_API_KEY and ITCH_USER, so on a runner with those set the child found the real paid build, resolved the live store page and called butler. It failed here only because the local key was not valid, so nothing was uploaded, but the path to a real upload was open. The in-process part of the same test cleared ip.USER only, and the upload path uses the API key, so that guard did not hold either.
evidence: running the child with the itch.io and butler variables stripped still reached butler and printed 'creating build on remote server: itch.io API error (400): /wharf/builds: invalid target (bad user)', which is a remote call made before the run failed
repro: start itch_publish.py with no itch.io credentials but with a paid build present and watch whether butler is reached
fix: the test scrubs the credentials from every child it starts, and itch_publish.upload() now refuses before running butler when there is no itch.io user, naming the variable that is missing
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py starts every child with the scrubbed environment and asserts that upload() starts no process at all when there is no user
verification: with the credentials stripped the child no longer reaches butler; removing the guard from upload() makes the new check fail, so it bites.

symptom: the test suite could have spent real model money
root_cause: audit_selftest.py ran improve_daily.py in a copied directory with the inherited environment. A copied directory protects the files, not the API: improve_daily calls the model provider, the provider reads GROQ_API_KEY from the environment, and the scheduled lane that runs audit_selftest.py has a real one. The check that a module survives a missing data file was therefore making a real, billable request.
evidence: the sanitised environment was applied to the first improve_daily run only; the run at line 81, inside the loop over six modules, inherited everything, and the lane that runs this test sets GROQ_API_KEY
repro: run audit_selftest.py with a GROQ_API_KEY set and watch whether a request is made
fix: every child a test starts now gets the environment from testenv, which takes out the provider keys and the service credentials, and the runners that start the whole suite scrub the environment for their children as well
regression_test: selftest_audit.py now reads the source of every selftest and fails when one starts a child process with the inherited environment, or with an environment copied from os.environ
verification: a fresh venv with requests alone shows the lane failing on the missing module; the static check reports zero problems across 140 files, and removing the env= from one call makes it report that one file

symptom: the test suite destroyed the rate limit and the budget that protect it
root_cause: selftest.py and audit_selftest.py tested the token meter by resetting it and adding to it, and they did that against the real data directory, so the recorded spend was zeroed and the guard that decides whether the pipeline may spend was disarmed for the rest of the month. audit_selftest.py did the same to the real budget file, writing invalid content over it and restoring it afterwards, so a run killed in between left the allowance unreadable, which refuses every job. Its backup was written next to the real file as data/budget.json.auditbak, which nothing ignores, so a git add -A could commit the allowance.
evidence: both tests are run by the scheduled lanes, and tokenmeter.STATE and budget.STATE are module-level paths into the real data directory
repro: run selftest.py and audit_selftest.py and look at whether the real token_usage.json and budget.json are touched
fix: both tests now work on their own files in a temporary directory, and the budget backup is written outside the repository
regression_test: the meter check in selftest.py points tokenmeter.STATE at a temporary file and restores it; the budget check points budget.STATE at a temporary file and removes the directory afterwards
verification: the tests pass, and the real data directory is unchanged afterwards

symptom: the shop sold thirty-two products as a Full edition for nothing
root_cause: groupProducts dropped every catalogue entry marked published:false before grouping it with its family. For a product whose paid edition is not on sale yet, the entry that is marked false is the paid one, so the family was left holding only the free edition and `full` fell back to it. The card then read 'Full edition' and took the free edition's price, which is zero. The dialog offered a 'Get the full edition' button that charged nothing, and the checkout link carried the free edition's slug because it read item.base_slug, a property groupProducts never set. On the live site that was thirty-two of the thirty-four products; only the two that are actually on sale were right.
evidence: running the live page's own groupProducts and render against the live apps.json gave 34 cards, 32 of them labelled 'Full edition' and priced $0.00, with the title still carrying the '(Basic)' suffix
repro: load the page and read what the cards say
fix: groupProducts keeps both editions and records whether the paid one is on sale. A product that is not for sale yet is shown as the free edition it actually is, at its real price, and the dialog offers the free download and says the paid edition is still being prepared.
regression_test: site_js_selftest.py checks the grouping in a real browser: a product with an unsold paid edition is still listed, is not treated as on sale, and shows the free edition
verification: the old grouping fails all three of the new checks; the new one renders 34 cards of which 0 claim to be a Full edition at a free price

symptom: a paid app did nothing at all, on the live site
root_cause: One stray brace in the script block that had been appended to the chess-board app made the whole file fail to parse, so the app showed no board, no buttons and no error the visitor could see. It was in the catalogue that whole time. The validator that refuses a broken app could not see it, because it could not read a template literal: it reported eleven perfectly good apps as unparseable instead.
evidence: loading the file in a real browser gave 'SyntaxError: missing ) after argument list' and an empty page, in both the free and the paid edition
repro: load the app in a browser and look for a board
fix: the stray brace is gone, the validator reads template literals properly, and tier_gate_selftest.py checks that every app's script parses
regression_test: the validator reports the broken file as 'a } closes the wrong bracket' and none of the thirty-four apps as unparseable; the selftest fails when the brace is put back
verification: the app now renders its 64 squares in both editions, and the free one has no export control while the paid one does

symptom: the paid features were not gated, or were gated the wrong way round
root_cause: Ten apps had a paid feature that the free edition could use, a paid feature the paid edition could not use, or a limit that was never applied. The chess-board export control was created only in the free edition, because the gate asked whether the limit was unlimited. The split-bill import button was hidden in both editions, because LIM never defined the key it asked for. The dev-converter data section was never shown. The regex-tester limit check compared !TIER with 'full', which can never be true. Nine apps offered import with no cap, so the free edition could import more than the limit it advertises. Two apps declared a limit they never used, so the limit was not a limit.
evidence: checked in a real browser: the free edition of dev-converter has no data section, the split-bill import button is hidden with the paid edition, and speed-typing-test never applies its limit of three
repro: look at each app's gate in the free edition and the paid one
fix: each gate now asks whether the capability exists rather than whether the limit is unlimited, every limit key LIM uses is defined, and every import is capped at the edition's limit
regression_test: tier_gate_selftest.py checks that no tier comparison can never be true, that every LIM key used is defined, and that no feature is gated on the limit instead of the capability
verification: re-introducing the broken comparison, the undefined key and the wrong gate each makes the selftest fail

symptom: the command that puts a product on the store also put it on the free edition
root_cause: set_itch_url.set_url() wrote the store URL onto both editions of a product. The free edition is a download from this site and has never been uploaded to itch.io, so a store URL on it is a claim that is not true, and the site then offers a buy button for something that is free. set_all() and itch_publish.record() both strip it from the free tier, and the release instructions tell the operator to run this command, so running them as written produced exactly the state the audit had closed.
evidence: the docstring of set_all() says the free editions are deliberately not given a store URL, and set_url() did the opposite
repro: run set_itch_url.py with a product and look at both of its entries
fix: set_url() clears the store URL from the free edition and sets it on the paid one, which is what the other two writers do
regression_test: itchurl_selftest.py checks that no free edition in the catalogue carries a store URL, and that the command itself does not put one there
verification: the check fails when the guard is removed from set_url()

symptom: one environment variable put a buy button on every free product
root_cause: pricing.py filled in every catalogue entry without an itch_url from the ITCH_PAGE_URL environment variable, including the free editions. The comment above it says there is no fallback and that an empty value means 'not for sale yet', but the line was still there. The test that guards this could not see it, because it looks for a literal URL and this is a value read at run time, so setting the variable put a store URL on all thirty-four free editions at once.
evidence: the comment and the code disagreed, which is how it survived the audit that removed the hardcoded version of the same thing
repro: set ITCH_PAGE_URL and run pricing.py
fix: the fallback is only used for a paid edition, and only when the value is a real product page and not the account's front page
regression_test: itchurl_selftest.py reads the syntax tree and fails if any module fills itch_url from the environment
verification: the check fails when the environment read is put back

symptom: the tool that brings a dead product back on sale could not
root_cause: rebuild_paid.py existed to reconstruct a product whose paid build is missing and put it back on sale. It called build_exe.main(), and build_exe has make_ico() and build_app() and no main(), so it died with an AttributeError after it had already written the product out. It also compared the slug against the installer's file name, and the installer is named after the product's title, so it refused the correct installer for every product. And it handed butler the store's URL where butler wants the project's slug, so the target could not have worked even if the build had.
evidence: build_exe.main() does not exist; 'password-manager' would be 'Offline password manager-Setup.exe' and the slug is not a substring of the file name once the dashes are removed
repro: run rebuild_paid.py for a product and watch it fail
fix: it builds the installer the way the Friday job does, compares the installer by slug or title the way the publisher does, and gives butler the project slug
regression_test: paidbuild_selftest.py checks all three, and the full path was run: the installer built, was verified as this product's, and the upload was refused because there was no itch.io user
verification: removing any one of the three makes the selftest fail

symptom: the free edition's folder was named twice over
root_cause: make_app.main() passed an already-suffixed slug to write_app, which appends '-basic' itself, so the free edition was written to '<slug>-basic-basic'. The published copy the catalogue links to stayed stale, a duplicated slug was published to GitHub Pages, and the release gate refused the build. The other two callers already passed the plain slug for exactly this reason.
evidence: stage_app.py and verify_app.py both carry a comment saying the suffix is added by write_app, and main() did the opposite
repro: call write_app with a suffixed slug and look at the folder name
fix: main() passes the plain slug, and write_app accepts either form and adds the suffix once
regression_test: paidbuild_selftest.py writes both editions into a temporary directory and checks that both are called '<slug>-basic'
verification: removing the guard from write_app makes the selftest fail

symptom: the command that puts a product on sale proved it with another product's build
root_cause: publish_paid.py decided a product was on sale by looking for the words download, Buy or purchase in the body of the itch.io page. The store is ONE project holding every product, and that page says 'download' for every slug forever, so the check passed for a product whose build had never been uploaded. The catalogue was then marked published and the site offered a buy button for a product with nothing behind it. The publisher had the right check all along, build_is_listed, which looks for this product's own installer by name.
evidence: the live store page contains 'download' and 'purchase' for every product, and 'Markdown editor-Setup.exe' is not listed on it at all, so the old check would have published a product with no build
repro: run publish_paid.py for a product that was never uploaded
fix: the product's own installer has to be listed on the page, by name, and the price rule is checked before the catalogue is written
regression_test: itchpublish_selftest.py and itchurl_selftest.py cover the catalogue rules; the check is in the publisher, which is the one place that decides
verification: a product with no build of its own on the page is refused, and the refusal says which names it looked for

symptom: the release gate let a paid build through
root_cause: check_exposure.py is the last thing between the paid product and the public site, and it had three holes. It looked for a flat index.html, but the paid edition is paid/<slug>/app/index.html, so a copy of the paid folder into site/apps/ was invisible to it. It read the folder check's exemption from data/candidate.json and allowed the plain paid slug with it, so the folder holding the paid build was accepted as a known basic edition. And its list of development files had no binary extensions, so the installer, which is the paid product, was not on it.
evidence: five leaks were reproduced against the real gate: a paid build at apps/<slug>/app/, the same with a candidate naming that slug, a flat paid build, a paid edition inside the basic folder, and an installer under site/downloads. The gate printed 'ok' for all five.
repro: put a paid build in the published folder and run the gate
fix: the gate looks for the paid build in the app folder as well, reads the tier constant in the file, only exempts the free edition's folder name, and refuses any binary under the published site
regression_test: audit_selftest.py builds a public site with each leak in it and asks the gate about it
verification: all five leaks are now caught; the old gate passed all five

symptom: a version with two numbers was silently thrown away
root_cause: parse() returned (1, 0, 0) for any version with fewer than three parts, so `update_state.py --set 2.0` stored version 1.0.0, logged 'version 1.0.0' and exited 0. The release state moved backwards and the run reported success.
evidence: parse('2.0') gave (1, 0, 0), and the same fallback meant the installed version of any app was normalised to 1.0.0
repro: run update_state.py --set 2.0 and read the state file
fix: a version with fewer than three parts is padded with zeros, and only a version with no digits in it is the unknown 1.0.0
regression_test: update_selftest.py checks the padding, the empty case and a bump on a short version
verification: restoring the old parse makes the new checks fail

symptom: an installed app could never be told it was out of date
root_cause: installed_version() read app.json from one level too high for the launcher, which passes the app's root while the file is in the app folder inside it, so the installed version was always the fallback of 1.0.0. The banner then said '1.0.0 is installed' for a copy that was already current and could never stop. And latest() read a local site/update.json, which is gitignored and was never in the bundle, so for a customer it always returned nothing and the banner could never appear at all. The per-app version map was kept in the state file and never published, so a product could not learn its own version even in principle.
evidence: the launcher reads BASE/app/app.json and the check read BASE/app.json, and no build step put an app.json in the bundle at all
repro: run app_update.py against an installed layout
fix: both places the file can be are tried, the published file is fetched when there is no local copy, and the per-app versions are published
regression_test: update_selftest.py checks that the installed version is read from either layout
verification: the old function returns 1.0.0 for the layout the launcher uses

symptom: a product's title and price came from whichever edition was listed first
root_cause: _describe() took the first catalogue entry with a matching slug and stopped there, so a family written basic-first described the product as the free edition, with its price of zero, and the caller then quietly substituted the default price of $3.00. The site advertised the catalogue price and itch.io charged the substituted one. It also asked for entry['full'], a nested shape the catalogue does not have, so the branch it took always found nothing.
evidence: _describe on a synthetic basic-first family gave ('thing', 0.0), and on a full-first family gave the right answer
repro: describe a product whose family is listed basic-first
fix: the paid entry is found whichever order the family is in, the same way the rest of the module does it
regression_test: the publisher's own tests cover the catalogue rules
verification: a basic-first family now gives the same answer as a full-first one

symptom: verifying an app destroyed the paid build that was already there
root_cause: write_app emptied the paid folder before writing to it, and the paid folder holds the installer, which took forty minutes to build. Verifying an app on a machine that already had the paid build destroyed that build, silently, because paid/ is gitignored and nothing showed it in a diff. It also meant the verify job's artifact could never carry the installer, so the installer job always rebuilt it from nothing.
evidence: write_app did rmtree(PAID_DIR / slug) for the full tier
repro: run verify_app.py with a paid build present and look at the folder
fix: only the two files write_app owns are replaced, and the rest of the folder is left alone
regression_test: the layout checks in paidbuild_selftest.py cover the folder naming
verification: the paid folder and its installer survive a rewrite

symptom: a rejected candidate stayed staged for ever
root_cause: verify_app.py removed data/candidate.json only when the app passed. A rejected candidate stayed in a tracked file, so the next run verified the same rejected app again, and it kept widening the release gate's exemption for that folder name for as long as it existed.
evidence: the unlink was on the success path only
repro: reject an app and look for the candidate file
fix: the candidate is cleared whether the app passed or not
regression_test: the file is gone either way
verification: putting the unlink back leaves it behind on the failure path

symptom: the paid edition never said what the customer was paying for
root_cause: The generator's raw path asks the model for the app file and nothing else, and the three things that describe the product to a customer, its name, the list of what the paid edition adds and the two descriptions, were set to empty strings. Every product was published with the same description as its own free edition and an empty differences list, so the shop asked for three dollars and never said what the three dollars were for. The answer was in the app's own limit table, which nobody read.
evidence: the live catalogue has an identical blurb and an empty differences list for both editions of all thirty-four products, and the buy dialog shows that blurb
repro: look at what the paid option says in the buy dialog
fix: the paid features are read out of the app's own limit table, which costs no model call, and a feature is only claimed if the app is seen to have it, so nothing is promised that is not there
regression_test: tier_gate_selftest.py checks that every product's paid edition has something the free one does not
verification: all thirty-four products now list real differences, and a limit key with no matching control is not claimed

symptom: the bot cannot read the server's channels
root_cause: The Discord guild routes answer 403 for this bot: the member record, the channel list and the role list all return 'internal network error' with code 40333, which is Discord's Unknown Member. The token itself is good, it is in the guild, and the webhook posts fine, so this is on Discord's side of the connection rather than in the code. It needs a person with access to the server.
evidence: run 39674190056: 'discord bot - Slingshot Tools#2486' and 'discord server - Slingshot Tools' both PASS, the webhook PASSES, and only the guild-scoped routes answer 403 with code 40333
repro: run check-connections.yml and read the discord channels row
fix: not a code change. A person with access to the server should check the bot's permissions and re-invite it if the membership record is stale. The posting path is unaffected, because the webhook is tried first and it works.
regression_test: check_connections.py already reports what Discord actually returned, so the failure is actionable as it stands
verification: not verified, because it cannot be fixed from here and the fix needs access to the Discord server. It may also be a Discord-side outage, in which case it clears itself. Until then the connections lane stays red on this one row, and only on this one row.

symptom: the YouTube refresh token was revoked
root_cause: The stored YouTube refresh token no longer exchanges for an access token, which is what happens when a Google account revokes the authorisation, when the app is in testing mode and the refresh token has expired, or when the consent screen is changed. Re-authorising is an interactive browser step with a Google account, so it cannot be done from here.
evidence: run 39674190056: 'FAIL youtube - the refresh token was revoked or expired', and the check itself says 'run python shorts_auth.py again'
repro: run check-connections.yml and read the youtube row
fix: not a code change. A person has to run python shorts_auth.py and complete the Google consent screen, then put the new refresh token in the YOUTUBE_REFRESH_TOKEN secret.
regression_test: check_connections.py says exactly what to do, so the failure is actionable as it stands
verification: not verified, because re-authorising needs a browser and a Google account. Nothing in the shop depends on it. The lanes that publish to YouTube would fail on their own, and they are not part of a release.

symptom: the guard that protects the site could not see anything
root_cause: changed_files() asked git for the diff between HEAD and HEAD with the three-dot form, which is a merge-base comparison, so the merge base was that commit and the diff was empty with exit code 0. The function always returned an empty list, the fallback that would have caught it was unreachable, and every gate built on it reported '0 changed file(s), none protected' while a protected workflow sat modified in the tree. Six workflows run that gate, and self_upgrade.py asks the same question after a patch.
evidence: with a protected workflow modified in the tree, git reported the file as changed, changed_files() returned an empty list, violations() returned nothing and guard() returned 0
repro: modify a protected file and run python weekly_guard.py check
fix: the working tree against HEAD, and anything staged, is what is asked about, and a job that commits its own change asks before it commits
regression_test: audit_selftest.py modifies a protected workflow, asks the guard, and checks that it sees the file, calls it a violation and refuses
verification: putting the three-dot form back makes all three checks fail

symptom: the repair lane could rewrite the scripts the guard protects
root_cause: The repair lane's allow-list included build_exe.py and build_installer_app.py, and both are in the guard's list of the scripts that make the site work, so the lane could rewrite the very files the guard exists to protect and the gate would not have said so, because the gate was not looking. The lane also only compiled the patched file and stopped, though its own docstring said a patch must survive a test run, so a whole-file rewrite that broke the build but still parsed was committed to main and pushed. It also had itself in the allow-list.
evidence: the two files were in both lists, and no test ran anywhere in the file
repro: ask the repair lane to patch a protected script and see what it does
fix: a protected file is never repairable, the whole suite has to pass with the patch in place, and the guard has the last word before anything is committed
regression_test: audit_selftest.py asks the repair lane about a protected script and checks that it is refused
verification: removing the refusal makes the check fail

symptom: a credential held as a dictionary value was written to the public log
root_cause: The scrubber needed the name and the value side by side in one string, and in a dictionary they are two separate strings, so a credential held as a value was written to the log as it was. The log is a tracked file in a public repository, and the natural place for a credential is the evidence dictionary every event carries. The test that claimed to cover it passed only because its nested value happened to match a shape rule.
evidence: scrub({'password': 'hunter2000'}) returned the password unchanged, and the same for an itch.io session cookie, a Discord bot token and an authorization header
repro: scrub a dictionary holding a credential
fix: a key that names a credential means the value is one, however ordinary the value looks, and the value is replaced
regression_test: audit_selftest.py checks that a password, a session cookie, a Discord token, an authorization header and a nested key are all replaced, and that an ordinary word is not
verification: removing the replacement makes the checks fail

symptom: rotating the audit log threw the history away
root_cause: The rotation copied the newest file to .1 and then deleted it, which is the opposite of what its own docstring says it does, and read() only ever read the newest file, so past the size limit the whole trail became empty and the report that depends on it reported nothing.
evidence: with the size limit lowered, the log file did not exist afterwards and read() returned no events
repro: write more than the size limit worth of events and read them back
fix: the newest file is emptied rather than deleted, and the rotated files are read too, oldest first, so the trail is continuous
regression_test: audit_selftest.py writes past the limit and checks the file is still there and there is still something to read
verification: deleting the file instead of emptying it makes the check fail

symptom: the price engine reset the whole shop to the starting price every week
